passage: I'm Disha, Mehak's roommate. She asked me to sit two tables away at the tea shop near Sector 17, 'just in case'. Her father arrived early, holding a box of pinnis, which she used to love. They didn't hug. He said something and she nodded; later she told me they'd agreed not to talk about the fight today. For forty minutes they discussed her exams, his new scooter, the rain. Near the end she said something slowly, looking at her cup. He looked up, and his eyes were wet. He answered. When they left, he paid, and she let him. She told me afterwards she'd said, 'I missed you,' and he'd said, 'I was wrong to shout.' They still disagree about most things, she said. But they're meeting again next month.

qa.q: What was Mehak's father holding when he arrived?
qa.a: He was holding a box of pinnis.

qa.q: What might Mehak's father have felt when she spoke into her cup, judging by his wet eyes?
qa.a: He seems moved and relieved to hear 'I missed you', perhaps after months of fearing she didn't.

qa.q: Why was agreeing not to talk about the fight a wise rule for this first meeting?
qa.a: It kept the meeting short and safe, so each could say one true thing without the old argument taking over; harder topics can wait.

qa.q: How does Disha see the meeting from two tables away?
qa.a: She watches carefully without knowing their feelings for sure, noticing cues like the pinnis, the wet eyes and Mehak letting him pay 🙂.

grounding: A roommate watches a young woman and her father meet for tea, set the past aside for the day and each say one true thing.

passage:
Tuesday. Vikas typed and deleted the message four times before sending it: 'Tea on Saturday? Just an hour. Can we not talk about last year yet?' Sunaina replied within a minute: 'Yes. Just tea.'
Saturday. At the café near the bus depot, they both ordered masala chai and stirred too long. They talked about his internship, her new job, the neighbour's noisy dog. Before leaving, Vikas said, 'I'm proud of the work I'm doing, Ma. I wanted you to know.' Sunaina said, 'I've kept your room the same. I don't know if that's good or bad.' Neither pushed further.
Wednesday. A photo arrived on Vikas's phone: two cups of chai on her kitchen table. 'Next Saturday?' He wrote back, 'Yes.' Then, a minute later: 'Still don't agree with you about everything.' 'I know,' she replied. 'Come anyway.'

qa.q: How many times did Vikas type and delete the message before sending it?
qa.a: He typed and deleted it four times before sending it.

qa.q: What did Sunaina mean by saying she doesn't know if keeping his room the same is good or bad?
qa.a: She seems unsure whether it shows love or an inability to let go, and she chose to share that uncertain, true feeling rather than a neat one.

qa.q: Which choices made this reunion work in small steps?
qa.a: A one-hour limit, leaving last year for later, each saying one true thing, and agreeing to meet again without needing full agreement.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel when Sunaina replies 'Come anyway'?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and welcomed, seeing that his mother wants him to visit even though they still disagree.

grounding: Over a week a young man and his mother meet for a short tea, avoid the past, share one true thing each, and grow closer without full agreement.
